## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/02.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Update on Academic Impact Analysis and Report
• We last met in Fall, 2021 and discussed findings.
• The results from RICAS and WIDA-ACCESS in 2021 indicated overall academic
impact was moderate/large in ELA and large in mathematics.
• Both status-based analyses as well as growth-based analyses support these
findings.
• Since then we have finalized results associated with:
• RICAS spring 2021 summative assessment
• WIDA-ACCESS 2021 summative assessment
• Today we want to share results associated with the analyses.

Pandemic Related Academic Impact in Rhode Island 2</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/03.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">How do we quantify academic impact using test data
• The pandemic was like a “headwind” that (presumably) slowed down the learning of
students due to a variety of factors.
• We can use test data in two ways to quantify the impact of this headwind:
• Best way: Quantify how much the rate of learning (i.e., growth) slowed:
• RICAS: Use historical skip-year growth norms to quantify growth and compare to pre-COVID growth.
• ACCESS: Use historical consecutive-year growth norms and compare to pre-COVID growth
• Next best way: Look at how much 2021 status changed:
• RICAS: Use 2019 status (or some adjustment thereof) as a proxy.
• ACCESS: Use 2020 status (or some adjustment thereof) as a proxy.
• Adjustments include (potentially) imputation for missing data.
• Growth is to Speedometer as Status is to Odometer
• Growth deceleration/acceleration will show up as status decreases/increases and vice-versa

Pandemic Related Academic Impact in Rhode Island 3</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/04.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">How do we quantify academic impact using test data
• Status (odometer) comparisons are the most prevalent way of quantifying academic impact:
• Usually looking at decrease in percent proficient (e.g., grade 3 ELA 2019 to grade 3 ELA 2021)
• This isn’t wrong conceptually, just not the most refined metric to use.
• Strength: Status comparisons can be calculated for all grades and content areas and groups.
• Weakness: Status comparisons look at two distinct groups of students and don’t take account of system
improvement.
• Growth (speedometer) comparisons are less prevalent way of quantifying academic impact:
• Historical consecutive and skip-year growth norms were created for RICAS and ACCESS in May, 2021 for
use with 2021 RICAS and ACCESS data.
• Strength: Better accuracy as it only looks at one cohort of students.
• Weakness: Not available for all students since it requires a prior score.
• Rhode Island participation rates were below normal, with participation in elementary grades near 90%
decreasing to 80% in middle school grades.
• Participation (as we’ll see) has a bigger impact upon status comparisons than growth.
Pandemic Related Academic Impact in Rhode Island 4</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/13.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Review of results: RICAS
• Academic impacts in mathematics were larger than those in ELA,
though impacts were large in both content areas.
• Academic impacts were larger in middle school grades than
elementary school grades.
• Across demographic subgroups, academic impacts were generally
large to severe.
• When impacts for subgroups are small, questions about pre-pandemic
rates of learning come under suspicion.

Pandemic Related Academic Impact in Rhode Island 13</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/16.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Review of results: WIDA-ACCESS
• For English Language Learners taking the WIDA-ACCESS English
• Academic impacts were moderate to large for students in the
elementary and middle school grades.
• Academic impacts were modest to none for students in the high
school grades.
• These results are fairly consistent with the seven other WIDA states
we examine.

Pandemic Related Academic Impact in Rhode Island 16</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/17.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">RICAS results for larger districts
• Like with demographic subgroups earlier, we can examine academic
impact by district.
• The following plots show academic impact results for several larger
districts.
• Given the large size of the academic impact overall, most districts
experienced large to severe impacts.
• There is, however, variability to be seen in the results.

Pandemic Related Academic Impact in Rhode Island 17</div>
```
